title: Geologic Processes

competencies.text: Describe volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis. Describe slow processes: soil erosion, saltwater intrusion.

days.title: Volcanic Eruptions
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

This week you will describe fast geologic processes — volcanic eruptions, earthquakes and tsunamis — and slow processes such as soil erosion and saltwater intrusion.

🌋 Why Volcanoes Erupt

Magma contains dissolved gases. As it rises and pressure drops, the gases form bubbles (like opening a softdrink). If the magma is thick and gas-rich, pressure builds until it bursts out explosively. Runny, gas-poor magma flows out more gently.

Eruption styleFeaturesExample
EffusiveLava flows, little ashSome of Mayon's lava-flow phases
ExplosiveAsh columns, pyroclastic flowsPinatubo 1991, Taal 2020
PhreaticSteam-driven blast when water meets hot rockSeveral Taal and Kanlaon events

⚠️ Volcanic Hazards

  • Pyroclastic flows — fast, ground-hugging clouds of hot gas and rock; deadliest hazard.
  • Ashfall — damages lungs, crops and roofs.
  • Lahars — volcanic mudflows when rain mixes with loose ash (Pinatubo lahars buried towns for years).
  • Volcanic gases — such as sulfur dioxide (vog).

PHIVOLCS uses alert levels 0–5; higher numbers mean an eruption is more likely or ongoing.

✅ Quick Check

3 questions — read each explanation.

scenario.text: What MOST directly causes an explosive volcanic eruption?

choices.label: Gas pressure building up in thick magma
Rainwater cooling the top of the volcano
Strong winds pushing on the crater rim

scenario.explanation: Dissolved gases expand as magma rises; in thick magma they cannot escape easily, so pressure builds until it explodes.

scenario.text: Which volcanic hazard is a fast-moving cloud of hot gas and rock fragments?
scenario.explanation: Pyroclastic flows race down slopes at very high speed and temperature and are the deadliest volcanic hazard.

scenario.text: Months after an eruption, heavy rain sends mud and debris down a volcano's rivers. What is this called?
scenario.explanation: Lahars form when rain mobilizes loose volcanic ash and debris into fast mudflows.

days.title: Earthquakes and Tsunamis
days.content:
🌎 What Is an Earthquake?

Rocks along a fault lock together while plates keep moving. Stress builds until the rocks suddenly slip, releasing energy as seismic waves. Most Philippine earthquakes are tectonic; some are volcanic.

TermMeaning
Focus (hypocenter)Point underground where the rupture starts
EpicenterPoint on the surface directly above the focus
MagnitudeEnergy released (one number per quake)
IntensityStrength of shaking and damage at a place (PHIVOLCS Earthquake Intensity Scale I–X)

🌊 Tsunamis

A tsunami is a series of very long sea waves, usually caused by an undersea earthquake that suddenly moves the sea floor up or down. Other causes include undersea landslides and eruptions. Natural warning signs: strong shaking near the coast, a sudden drop or rise of sea level, and a roaring sound from the sea. Move to high ground immediately — do not wait for an official warning.

🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each term to its meaning. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

match.right: Surface point directly above the focus
match.why: Shaking is often strongest near it.

match.right: Amount of energy released by a quake
Strength of shaking at a specific place
match.why: It varies with distance and ground type.

match.right: Series of long waves from sea-floor movement
match.why: Most are caused by undersea earthquakes.

match.right: Natural warning sign of a tsunami
match.why: Go to high ground at once.
It issues alerts and hazard maps.

days.title: Slow Processes: Erosion and Saltwater Intrusion
days.content:
🐢 Slow but Serious

Not all geologic hazards are sudden. Some act over years and decades, so they are easy to ignore until damage is large.

🌧️ Soil Erosion

Erosion removes topsoil through rain, flowing water and wind. Heavy tropical rain on bare, steep slopes is especially damaging. Causes include deforestation, slash-and-burn (kaingin), overgrazing and quarrying. Effects: less fertile farmland, muddy rivers, silted dams and reefs, more flooding and landslides. Solutions: reforestation, contour farming, terracing, cover crops and grass strips.

🧂 Saltwater Intrusion

Near the coast, fresh groundwater floats above denser salty groundwater. When wells pump too much fresh water, seawater moves inland underground. Sea-level rise and land subsidence (sinking ground, often from over-pumping) make it worse — parts of coastal Bulacan, Pampanga and Metro Manila are sinking. Effects: salty wells, failing crops, corroded pipes. Solutions: limit pumping, use surface water and rainwater, recharge aquifers, protect mangroves.

🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Decide what to do in real situations. Read every explanation. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

scenario.text: PHIVOLCS raises Taal Volcano to Alert Level 4. What does this mean for residents near the volcano?

choices.label: A hazardous eruption may come within days — evacuate
The volcano has become quiet and is safe for visitors again
Only boats on the lake need to move, while homes are safe
The volcano is extinct and will never erupt again

scenario.explanation: Alert Level 4 means a hazardous explosive eruption is possible soon. Residents in the danger zone must evacuate.

scenario.text: At the beach after strong shaking, the sea suddenly pulls far back, exposing the sea floor. What should you do?

choices.label: Run to high ground right away
Walk out to collect fish and shells
Wait on the shore for an announcement
Take photos from the edge of the water

scenario.explanation: A sudden drop in sea level after an earthquake is a natural tsunami warning. The waves can arrive within minutes.

scenario.text: A hillside cleared for kaingin is losing soil every rainy season. Which solution addresses the CAUSE?

choices.label: Replant trees and use contour farming on the slope
Clear even more trees so the water can drain faster
Burn the remaining grass to make the soil firmer
Dig straight ditches running down the steepest slope

scenario.explanation: Roots and contour farming slow runoff and hold soil in place, reducing erosion at its source.

scenario.text: Coastal wells in a barangay become salty while nearby land slowly sinks. Which human activity MOST likely links both?
scenario.explanation: Pumping out too much groundwater lets seawater move in and also causes the ground to compact and subside.

scenario.text: A magnitude 7.2 earthquake strikes while you are in a classroom. What should you do DURING the shaking?

choices.label: Drop, cover under a sturdy desk, and hold on
Run outside immediately through the crowded hall
Stand near the windows to see what is happening
Use the elevator to get down to the ground floor

scenario.explanation: Drop, Cover and Hold protects you from falling objects. Running during shaking causes injuries; windows can shatter.

days.title: Reducing Geologic Risk
days.content:
🗺️ Know the Hazard

PHIVOLCS maps active faults (like the West Valley Fault through Metro Manila), volcano danger zones, tsunami and liquefaction areas. Communities use these maps to avoid building on fault traces or in lahar channels.

🏗️ Build Safely

  • Follow the National Building Code and structural code for earthquake-resistant design: reinforced concrete, proper steel bars, strong connections.
  • Avoid heavy, unreinforced hollow-block walls and overhanging loads.
  • Secure tall cabinets and water tanks.

🏫 Prepare

The Nationwide Simultaneous Earthquake Drill (NSED) trains schools and offices. Families should know evacuation routes, meeting points and emergency numbers. Coastal communities should know tsunami routes to high ground.

🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Lab

3 lives, 6 keys. You need 70% (5 of 6). Read each explanation.

choices.label: An undersea earthquake moving the sea floor
Strong typhoon winds blowing hard on the sea
Heavy rain falling far out in the ocean
The Moon pulling the tides much higher

escape.explanation: Sudden vertical movement of the sea floor during an undersea earthquake displaces a huge volume of water.

escape.text: What is the point on Earth's surface directly above an earthquake's focus called?
escape.explanation: The epicenter is directly above the focus (hypocenter), where the rupture begins.

escape.text: Which is a SLOW geologic process?
escape.explanation: Erosion acts gradually over years; the others happen in seconds to hours.

escape.text: Which agency monitors volcanoes, earthquakes and tsunamis in the Philippines?
escape.explanation: PHIVOLCS, under DOST, monitors geologic hazards and issues alerts.

escape.text: How is earthquake MAGNITUDE different from INTENSITY?

choices.label: Magnitude is energy; intensity is local shaking
Magnitude is shaking; intensity is total energy
They are two names for exactly the same value
Magnitude is only measured on the ocean floor

escape.explanation: Magnitude is one value for the energy released; intensity varies from place to place.

escape.text: What is the BEST action during strong earthquake shaking indoors?
escape.explanation: Drop, Cover and Hold under sturdy furniture protects you from falling and flying objects.
